bridges.description: Connect a divine cause and the claimed resurrection of Jesus to the existence of the Christian God.
Infer from beginning, change, or contingent existence to a necessary cause with divine attributes.
Use the earliest resurrection testimony, appearances, and empty-tomb tradition to identify the divine cause with Christianity.
Reconcile morally difficult biblical material with divine goodness through genre, context, permission, and divine authority over life.
Show that evil and nonbelief can coexist with God when they permit greater goods such as freedom.
Ground universal moral duties in a perfect universal person rather than social convention.
Argue that the specifically Christian God is unsupported or internally incompatible with the record attributed to that God.
Demand publicly discriminating evidence and compare divine-action claims with observable outcomes.
Challenge resurrection testimony through textual differences, source dependence, and natural or visionary alternatives.
Challenge whether the proposed first cause, pure actuality, and divine power explanations avoid the questions applied to the universe.
Compare asserted divine goodness with biblical violence, suffering, and institutional conduct attributed to Christianity.
Maintain that moral judgments can be objectively justified through real-world harm without a divine lawgiver.

sections.title: Origins, Change, and Necessary Explanation
sections.rationale: The affirmative's three generic-theism arguments supply the first major bridge to the motion, while the negative contests their concepts and explanatory stopping point.

sections.title: Resurrection and Textual Evidence
sections.rationale: The resurrection is the affirmative's stated bridge from generic theism to Christianity and receives sustained historical and textual challenge.

sections.title: Scriptural Morality and Interpretation
sections.rationale: Both speakers devote extensive argument to whether violent and morally difficult passages contradict the Christian God's goodness or admit contextual and nonliteral readings.

sections.title: Evil, Hiddenness, and Public Testing
sections.rationale: The exchange treats suffering, divine hiddenness, prayer, and the kind of evidence that could distinguish a God-governed world.

sections.title: Moral Grounding and Christian Institutions
sections.rationale: The speakers dispute the source of moral facts and whether church wrongdoing bears on a claimed institutional revelation.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The existence of God is a philosophical rather than a scientific question.
moves.warrant: Science supplies natural explanations for observable phenomena but does not by itself settle immaterial realities such as minds, moral truths, free will, or God.
moves.inference: The audience should assess philosophical arguments directly rather than require a scientific consensus or laboratory result.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact opening passage states the methodological claim and its examples without including the later cosmological arguments.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we are not discussing a scientific question
we have to look at the arguments for ourselves
moves.attributionRationale: It is within Horn's uninterrupted opening presentation.
moves.audioVerificationReason: None; the round and speaker are unambiguous.
moves.importanceRationale: It defines the evidential method used across Horn's case but does not itself establish the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It specifies how purportedly non-obvious divine reality should be assessed.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The universe's finite past requires an uncaused, timeless, immaterial, powerful personal cause.
moves.warrant: An actually traversed infinite series of past events would never reach today; a beginning requires a cause beyond space and time, and an immaterial chooser rather than an abstract object can initiate a temporal universe.
moves.inference: A cause bearing central divine attributes exists.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the complete first-cause chain from the finite-past premise through the personal-cause conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the past is finite and had a beginning
the cause of the universe must exist beyond space and time
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted opening case.
moves.importanceRationale: This is one of Horn's three stated foundations for a divine cause.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly supplies a first cause with divine attributes.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Present change requires a first actualizer that is pure actuality and possesses divine attributes.
moves.warrant: Potentials are actualized by something actual; an infinite instrumental series no more explains current change than infinitely many train cars explain motion without a locomotive, so the terminus has no unrealized potential.
moves.inference: An immaterial, timeless, necessary, powerful, knowing, and good actualizer exists even if the universe is temporally eternal.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The full passage is necessary because Horn moves from the act-potency account through the regress analogy to the attributes inferred from pure actuality.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: change is just the reduction of a potential to an actual
is just pure actuality
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted opening case.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Horn's argument designed to avoid dependence on a temporal beginning.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers an independent route from change to a divine actualizer.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The universe's contingent existence is explained by a necessary being rather than by nothing or an infinite series of dependent universes.
moves.warrant: Brute existence would undermine ordinary explanatory practice, the universe does not exist by definition, and adding dependent universes never supplies a nondependent explanation.
moves.inference: A necessary being of pure actuality explains why anything exists.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete three-option contingency argument and its necessary-being conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Why is there something rather than nothing?
there must be a necessary being
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted opening case.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the third independent generic-theism route in Horn's opening.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects contingent reality to a necessary divine explanation.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Jesus' bodily resurrection is the best explanation of early Christian testimony and the empty-tomb tradition.
moves.warrant: Paul reports individual, group, and skeptical witnesses; Jewish expectations disfavored a resurrected failed messiah; group experience, Paul's prior hostility, access to a Jerusalem tomb, and women as discoverers are offered against hallucination or invention.
moves.inference: The generic divine cause is identified with the Christian God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains Horn's entire Christianity-identification bridge and all four stated counters to the proposed hallucination hypothesis.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the best explanation for why Jesus' disciples preached Jesus' bodily resurrection
the tomb was empty
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted opening case.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Horn's explicit bridge from classical theism to the specifically Christian God.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly argues that resurrection evidence identifies Christianity as true.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Difficult descriptions of God and conquest commands need not be literal accounts of divine action or extermination.
moves.warrant: Scripture uses accommodated figurative descriptions; ancient theology can conflate direct causation with permission; and comparable ancient total-destruction language was used where the named people survived.
moves.inference: These passages do not by themselves establish a morally defective Christian God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage joins Horn's general accommodation account to his specific ancient-war-language example.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Dan also misunderstands the Bible's non-literal language
radical separation, not extermination
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted opening case.
moves.audioVerificationReason: None; unusual transliterations are not quoted.
moves.importanceRationale: It anticipates the central scriptural-morality objection developed by Barker.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies interpretive routes compatible with divine goodness.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Universal moral commands require a perfect universal person.
moves.warrant: Barker's moral criticism would not change with social opinion, while natural laws only describe what is and cannot command what ought to be.
moves.inference: Moral facts provide an additional argument for God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span is the complete compact moral argument, beginning with transcendence of society and ending with its proposed ground.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: morality isn't determined by society
moral commands must come from a perfect universal person
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted opening conclusion.
moves.importanceRationale: It is an additional theistic route and later becomes central to the moral exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies God as the source of binding moral facts.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The need to debate and argue for God is evidence against a God capable of direct revelation.
moves.warrant: A God who exists and wants belief could reveal itself directly rather than require human advocates and proofs.
moves.inference: Persistent non-obviousness counts against the Christian God's existence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The boundaries isolate Barker's opening hiddenness argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Why does God need arguments?
This very debate is one evidence against the existence of a God
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted opening presentation.
moves.importanceRationale: It introduces the later dispute over nonbelief and testability.

burdenContact.rationale: It treats expected public revelation as discriminating evidence.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Severe suffering, apparently chance-like prayer outcomes, and flourishing unbelievers count against a good and necessary God.
moves.warrant: Children die despite desperate prayers at rates Barker says resemble uncaring chance, while many people live moral and purposeful lives without belief.
moves.inference: Observed life lacks the expected protective and practical signature of the Christian God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact sequence contains Barker's problem-of-evil, prayer-outcome, and no-need claims without the subsequent biblical case.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Their children die at a rate no different from random, uncaring chance
good people lead loving, joyful, moral, charitable, purposeful, and hopeful lives
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies Barker's principal empirical case from suffering and divine inaction.

burdenContact.rationale: It compares observed suffering and prayer with outcomes expected under divine care.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The Christian God's biblical conduct is incompatible with the Bible's own claim that God is good.
moves.warrant: Barker cites commands and depictions involving conquest, killing children, punishment of descendants, execution for same-sex conduct, Job's suffering, harm to pregnant women, and texts calling divine acts evil.
moves.inference: A being characterized as both perfectly good and as producing these evil fruits is contradictory and cannot exist as described.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The long span is needed to preserve Barker's explicit good-tree inference and the representative biblical categories he uses to support it, rather than reducing the case to the adjective list.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit
Therefore the Christian God cannot exist
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted opening presentation.
moves.audioVerificationReason: None; potentially uncertain verse wording is paraphrased rather than silently normalized.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Barker's central specifically Christian nonexistence argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It alleges an internal conflict between perfect goodness and the scriptural record.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the interpretive defense by presenting multiple passages as direct words and actions attributed to God and by grounding the contradiction in the Bible's own good-fruit test.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Systemic clerical abuse and institutional cover-up count against the church as a revelation of a good Christian God.
moves.warrant: Barker distinguishes ordinary members from an institution that protected abusers and moved them to unsuspecting parishes.
moves.inference: A morally corrupt revelatory institution is unexpected if a good Christian God guides it.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span includes the international examples, the distinction between members and institution, and the conclusion bearing on divine revelation.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: has covered up the abuse and protected the rapists in their ranks
this would not be happening
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a distinct institutional-evidence line rather than Barker's primary scriptural contradiction.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests claimed divine revelation through the conduct of its institution.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Evil is logically compatible with God if God can bring a greater good from it.
moves.warrant: Freedom supplies one possible good reason for permitting moral evil, and Barker would have to exclude every possible divine reason to establish incompatibility.
moves.inference: The existence of suffering does not deductively refute God and moral duties invoked in the objection can instead support a moral source.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage includes the compatibility claim, free-will example, allocation of burden, and Horn's moral-duty reversal.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: God and evil are not logically incompatible
God allows moral evil so we can have free will
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted first rebuttal.
moves.audioVerificationReason: None; the transcript recognition of a name is not used.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Barker's principal suffering objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It gives a compatibility condition and an example of a greater good.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the inference from suffering to nonexistence by identifying freedom and other possible greater goods.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: God may permit nonbelief to preserve freedom in belief and action.
moves.warrant: Constantly obvious divine surveillance could alter free conduct, so non-obviousness may serve a greater good.
moves.inference: The existence of debate and nonbelief is not logically incompatible with God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage is Horn's complete direct reply to the opening hiddenness argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: God can allow non-belief
preserve greater goods like free will
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly addresses a central evidential expectation but is subsidiary to Horn's positive case.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies a proposed reason for divine hiddenness.

responseComponents.description: Disputes the expectation of direct revelation by proposing freedom-related reasons for non-obviousness.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The Bible's mixed genres and the narrative survival of targeted peoples support reading total-destruction commands nonliterally.
moves.warrant: A library can contain different genres without all being fiction, and the Amalekites continue in later generations despite language commanding that they be wiped out.
moves.inference: Barker cannot infer literal extermination merely from totalizing war language.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains both the genre analogy and the concrete internal-survival argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the Bible is like a library
they still carry on for many, many generations
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Horn's principal developed rebuttal to Barker's genocide texts.

burdenContact.rationale: It gives a source-internal basis for a nonliteral conquest reading.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the literal-extermination premise and the inference from selected passages to a contradiction in divine goodness.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Biblical language that God creates evil can refer to natural disaster rather than moral evil, and temporal pain can be accompanied by greater or eternal goods.
moves.warrant: Horn distinguishes the cited Hebrew usage from moral evil and argues that an all-powerful God can bring greater goods and infinite happiness from finite suffering.
moves.inference: The cited evil language and inflicted pain do not establish that God is morally evil.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage combines Horn's lexical-context reply with the compensating-good principle he uses for divine-caused suffering.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it refers to natural disasters, not moral evil
from that evil he can always bring greater goods
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted first rebuttal.
moves.audioVerificationReason: None; verse numbering and transliteration are not silently corrected in the move description.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers a recurring subset of Barker's scriptural examples.

burdenContact.rationale: It distinguishes kinds of evil and supplies a moral rationale for permitted harm.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the lexical equation of disaster with moral evil and the inference from finite suffering to divine malevolence.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Wrongdoing by church members does not show that the church's spiritual claims or benefits are false.
moves.warrant: A doctor's abuse does not justify abandoning hospitals or medicine; likewise corrupt users do not invalidate spiritual medicine.
moves.inference: The abuse scandal does not require leaving the Catholic Church or refute its divine role.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Horn's complete analogy responding to Barker's institutional challenge.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I won't stop going to hospitals
some people don't take the medicine
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly addresses the institutional argument but is not Horn's motion-level positive case.

burdenContact.rationale: It separates institutional misuse from the truth of the institution's religious claims.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the inference from corrupt personnel to falsity or worthlessness of the institution's saving function.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The resurrection narratives are internally inconsistent and lack independent historical corroboration.
moves.warrant: Barker says attempts to harmonize every detail fail, the five tellings do not fit together, and corroboration comes from believers rather than external history.
moves.inference: The resurrection story is weak evidence for God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Barker's complete first historical-textual challenge and his comparison to other religious miracle stories.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: The story has so many contradictions within it
It's just corroborated by believers
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests Horn's only bridge from generic theism to Christianity.

burdenContact.rationale: It attacks the reliability and independence of the resurrection sources.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the reliability and corroboration of the textual evidence supporting appearances and the empty tomb.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Horn misstates Barker as proposing a mass hallucination; grief-related inner experiences and other natural explanations remain possible.
moves.warrant: Barker distinguishes personally talking to a deceased loved one in the mind from a shared hallucination and says a plausible natural account blocks a forced leap to miracle.
moves.inference: Horn's rejection of group hallucination does not eliminate Barker's actual alternative.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage preserves the correction of attribution and Barker's own qualified alternative through its inferential consequence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I never said it was a grief-induced hallucination
you can explain it in naturalistic terms
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It identifies a mismatch between Horn's target and Barker's stated alternative.

burdenContact.rationale: It preserves a natural alternative after rejecting the shared-hallucination framing.

responseComponents.description: Disputes Horn's characterization of Barker's hypothesis and challenges the move from rejecting group hallucination to resurrection.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: An immaterial pure actuality cannot coherently possess power that produces physical change.
moves.warrant: Barker defines power as physical work over time and argues that interaction with the natural world brings a cause under physical attributes and laws.
moves.inference: Horn's divine-attribute conclusion from pure actuality contains a contradiction.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage isolates Barker's power objection from his following who-caused-God objection.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Power is work over time
if God is powerful, God is a physical being
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It targets the transition from an actualizer to an immaterial powerful being.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges a key divine-attribute inference.

responseComponents.description: Challenges whether immaterial pure actuality can exercise causal power over a physical world.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The explanatory demands used to infer God can be turned back on God's ordered mind.
moves.warrant: If functional complexity requires a designer or explanation, a nonrandom divine mind appears to require the same treatment.
moves.inference: Stopping explanation at God risks special pleading rather than completing the explanation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The boundaries contain Barker's explicit reversal and the divine-mind complexity example.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: even God himself would need an explanation
then so does the mind of that God
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It contests the explanatory stopping point shared by Horn's metaphysical arguments.

burdenContact.rationale: It asks whether the proposed explainer escapes the same explanatory principle.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the exemption of God from the demand for explanation.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The something-from-nothing premise is underdefined and physical vacua produce particles without an external divine cause.
moves.warrant: Barker argues that a pictured nothing is already something and cites particle-antiparticle emergence from quantum potential and black-hole radiation.
moves.inference: Horn's appeal to creation from nothing does not uniquely support God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage preserves Barker's definitional challenge and the full physical example he offers.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: what does the word nothing mean
something does come from nothing all the time
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It addresses the creation-from-nothing component rather than every premise of Horn's first-cause argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It contests the meaning and exclusivity of the creation premise.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the premise that beginning from nothing demands the kind of cause Horn infers.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Minor Gospel differences coexist with agreement on the empty tomb and appearances, while Christian resurrection claims arise earlier than later miracle legends.
moves.warrant: Horn lists the shared women-at-tomb, empty-tomb, and appearance core, treats differences as evidence against copying, and contrasts Christianity's origin story with later traditions about Muhammad.
moves.inference: Textual variation and comparison with other religions do not dissolve the resurrection's explanatory demand.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact span contains both parts of Horn's direct reply: shared core and early-origin comparison.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: what they agree on is far more important
at the core, very beginning of the Christian story
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly defends the central Christian-identification bridge.

burdenContact.rationale: It answers reliability and comparative-miracle objections.

responseComponents.description: Argues that shared core facts matter more than minor variation and that the resurrection claim is early rather than a late legend.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Quantum vacua are not nothing, and Horn's change argument concerns actualizing potential rather than relative spatial motion.
moves.warrant: A vacuum is a low-energy field with activity, while any reduction from potential to actual requires an actualizer; Horn also corrects Barker's attribution by stating God is pure actuality, not pure potential.
moves.inference: Barker's vacuum and relativity objections do not address the stated metaphysical premises.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains Horn's adjacent replies to Barker's two principal metaphysical objections and the corrected act-potency wording.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Quantum vacuums aren't nothing
I said he's pure actuality
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly repairs two alleged misunderstandings of Horn's central arguments.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the premises linking physical change and beginnings to a nonpotential cause.

responseComponents.description: Corrects the attribution of potentiality and distinguishes metaphysical actualization from relative motion.
Rejects the identification of an active low-energy field with nothing.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The corrupt-doctor analogy misses an institution-wide cover-up by an organization claimed as divine revelation.
moves.warrant: Barker distinguishes isolated bad actors from authorities allegedly moving and protecting abusers under institutional power.
moves.inference: Systemic church conduct remains evidence against the church's revelatory status even if individual Catholics are good.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Barker's complete distinction between individual wrongdoing and organized institutional protection.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: your analogy about the doctor and the pedophile priest is inapt
the church is culpable
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves the institutional argument after Horn's analogy.

burdenContact.rationale: It focuses the evidence on systemic institutional action linked to revelatory claims.

responseComponents.description: Argues that coordinated institutional protection, not merely individual corruption, is the relevant comparison.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Relabeling divine acts as disaster or bad events does not make them good, and Israelites are also portrayed as practicing the conduct used to condemn Canaanites.
moves.warrant: Barker connects the same source word to moral-evil contexts, emphasizes the harmful acts regardless of translation, and disputes a moral contrast between the groups.
moves.inference: Horn's lexical and comparative defenses do not resolve the moral objection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains Barker's lexical reply, his consequence-based fallback, and the parity response concerning child sacrifice.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: whatever you call it, God did it and it wasn't good
the Israelites themselves engaged in child sacrifice
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted second rebuttal.
moves.audioVerificationReason: None; the move preserves the source's uncertain verse reference without correcting it.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Horn's contextual-language defense with both lexical and substantive challenges.

burdenContact.rationale: It maintains the moral contradiction despite alternate labels and cultural comparisons.

responseComponents.description: Challenges both the lexical distinction and the claim that calling events disasters removes their moral significance.
Disputes the attempt to justify Israel's conduct by contrasting it with Canaanite child sacrifice.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: A specific prayer revealing hidden writing would provide falsifiable evidence for the claimed omniscient, prayer-answering God.
moves.warrant: Barker combines scriptural promises about receiving what believers ask, God's admitted knowledge of the hidden content, and Horn's claim that God answers prayer.
moves.inference: Declining the test weakens claims that the belief is publicly testable and that the cited prayer promises work as stated.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The mixed-speaker span is necessary to preserve Barker's proposed falsifier, Horn's admissions and qualification that God may say no, and Barker's stated consequence; removing either speaker would distort the exchange.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: what would convince me to change my mind
This is not a parlor trick
moves.attributionRationale: The complete turn sequence clearly identifies Barker proposing and defending the test while Horn supplies brief answers and objections.
moves.audioVerificationReason: None; attribution follows the explicit question-answer sequence.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies Barker's concrete answer to Horn's demand for falsifiability.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers a specific observation that Barker says would change his view.

responseComponents.description: Presses whether claimed prayer promises and omniscience can yield a concrete public disclosure rather than remain insulated by hidden reasons.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: If literal divinely ordered total killing qualifies as genocide, divine goodness must explain how such action could be good.
moves.warrant: Horn conditionally accepts that destroying a racial, ethnic, national, or religious group could meet the definition, then defines God as goodness without deficiency and appeals to immortal life beyond death.
moves.inference: The exchange tests whether Horn's definition of goodness answers the concrete moral content rather than merely redescribing God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The mixed passage preserves Barker's conditional setup, Horn's qualified definition admission, and Horn's substantive afterlife response; it ends before their separate utilitarian exchange.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: would you call that genocide?
God is good in the sense that he is the fullness of being itself
moves.attributionRationale: Barker clearly conducts this cross-examination and Horn's answers are required to state the challenged position accurately.
moves.audioVerificationReason: None; the turn sequence is explicit.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly probes the compatibility of the central biblical examples with divine goodness.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests the alleged contradiction using Horn's own conditional concessions and definition.

responseComponents.description: Asks what follows under the condition that the command is literal rather than nonliteral.
Tests whether afterlife compensation makes the stipulated act good.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Problematic passages do not overturn independently grounded belief in God and resurrection because they may be human additions, nonliteral, or exercises of God's authority over gifted mortal life.
moves.warrant: Horn treats God and resurrection as established independently, offers multiple textual explanations, and argues that a giver of life need not provide any fixed amount of mortal life before eternal existence.
moves.inference: Scriptural difficulty does not entail that the Christian God is nonexistent or evil.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Horn's full conditional reply from independent resurrection grounds through textual alternatives and the authority-over-life rationale.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are mere human additions to the Bible
if God gives us life, life is a gift from him
moves.attributionRationale: Within Barker-led cross-examination, the turn sequence clearly marks Horn's sustained answers, with Barker's questions providing necessary context.
moves.importanceRationale: It states Horn's broadest defense against the scriptural-morality inference.

burdenContact.rationale: It combines epistemic independence, interpretive alternatives, and divine authority over life.

responseComponents.description: Argues that independently supported theism and resurrection leave room for textual qualification rather than nonexistence.
Answers the concrete killing objection by invoking God's authority over the duration of mortal life and eternal continuation.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Morality follows universal natural-law facts grounded in God's perfect nature, not merely aggregate harm.
moves.warrant: Horn distinguishes human flourishing and nature from obeying arbitrary orders and gives torture for fun as wrong regardless of unanimous opinion.
moves.inference: Objective moral facts fit theism, while an atheistic account risks reducing them to changeable opinion.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage is Horn's concise positive moral theory and its contrast with atheism.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are universal moral principles
it is always wrong to torture a child for fun
moves.attributionRationale: The turn sequence in Barker-led cross-examination clearly identifies Horn's sustained answer.
moves.importanceRationale: It develops Horn's moral-grounding argument under direct questioning.

burdenContact.rationale: It states how universal moral facts flow from divine nature and natural law.

responseComponents.description: Clarifies the objective standard by which institutional acts can be condemned without making the institution's wrongdoing the source of morality.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Moral value can be objectively justified by real-world harm, and that standard condemns the treatment of Job despite promised compensation.
moves.warrant: Barker denies morality is mere opinion, says it can be measured against objective reality, and applies the criterion to Job's torture and the death of his children; Horn replies that infinite compensation can follow temporal bad.
moves.inference: A secular moral standard can make factual moral judgments and continues to challenge the goodness of attributed divine acts.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The mixed-speaker passage contains Barker's alternative grounding, his concrete Job test, and Horn's compensatory response needed to define the live disagreement.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a value that is justified by objective reality
was that a good thing to do?
moves.attributionRationale: The turn sequence clearly attributes the secular account and Job challenge to Barker and the final compensation answer to Horn.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests Horn's claim that atheism leaves only opinion and applies the alternative to the debate's moral evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers an objective-reality account and a concrete application.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the inference that objective moral judgments require a universal person.
Denies that atheism permits only opinion and proposes harm in objective reality as a basis.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The shared empty-tomb core and Paul's multiple appearance reports remain evidence for resurrection despite narrative differences.
moves.warrant: Horn says differences are minor, women's testimony is unlikely to be invented in that society, and Paul specifically reports appearances to Peter, James, groups, and five hundred.
moves.inference: Barker's textual and grief alternatives have not explained the full retained evidence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This closing passage independently restates the evidential premises it relies on, so it does not depend on excluded Q&A.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: They agree, as I said, on major details
Paul tells us specifically multiple times that Jesus appeared
moves.attributionRationale: It is Horn's uninterrupted closing statement after the approved gap.
moves.audioVerificationReason: None; the recognition form of the final number is not silently corrected.
moves.importanceRationale: It closes Horn's specifically Christian identification argument with independently stated evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It restates the empty-tomb and appearance evidence supporting resurrection.

responseComponents.description: Treats narrative differences as minor relative to the asserted shared core.
Appeals to multiple named and group appearances as evidence not covered by a private grief experience.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Women at the tomb are expected rather than embarrassing, and the tomb accounts differ on material details.
moves.warrant: Women ordinarily cared for tombs and brought spices, while accounts vary over which women arrived, timing, and whether the tomb was already open or opened in their presence.
moves.inference: The women detail does not independently authenticate the story, and discrepancies reduce testimonial credibility.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The closing states all supporting premises independently of the excluded Q&A and keeps the women and discrepancy replies together because they answer the same authenticity claim.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Women were always at the tombs
These are not trivial differences
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted closing statement.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Horn's final empty-tomb authenticity claims.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges both the embarrassment warrant and narrative consistency.

responseComponents.description: Argues that differences include material scene details rather than only inconsequential variation.
Challenges the claim that women witnesses are unlikely to be included unless the account is true.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The language and character of post-resurrection appearances, including Paul's experience, are consistent with visions rather than ordinary bodily encounters.
moves.warrant: Barker contrasts ordinary meeting vocabulary with repeated appearance language, describes vanishing episodes, and characterizes Paul's later encounter as visionary rather than physical.
moves.inference: Appearance reports do not by themselves establish a bodily resurrection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The closing independently states the linguistic and Pauline premises and therefore does not rely on excluded audience material.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: It was an appearance
He had a visionary experience
moves.attributionRationale: It is Barker's uninterrupted closing statement.
moves.audioVerificationReason: None; the Greek recognition is described without silently correcting its form.
moves.importanceRationale: It attacks the bodily character of the appearance evidence central to Horn's resurrection inference.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers a visionary interpretation of appearance testimony.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the inference from Paul's and others' reported appearances to bodily resurrection.

coverageAudit.omissionRationale: Closing repetitions are included only where they restate independent evidence or answer later objections; promotional book references are omitted.

coverageAudit.majorLine: Horn's treatment of difficult scripture through accommodation, genre, lexical context, and divine authority over life
coverageAudit.omissionRationale: Minor examples about descendants, sexual ethics, abortion rhetoric, and Job's pedagogical theme are omitted because the selected moves capture the load-bearing interpretive and moral defenses without exceeding section capacity.

coverageAudit.majorLine: Barker's opening burden, coherence, evidence, disagreement, evil, and hiddenness criticisms
coverageAudit.omissionRationale: The lack-belief definition, Nobel Prize analogy, denominational disagreement, ridicule, and generic definition objections are recorded as supporting or minor lines but omitted as separate moves because the selected public-evidence and suffering tests are the developed load-bearing versions.

coverageAudit.omissionRationale: The face-value/metaphor passage and individual examples are not separate rows because their claims are incorporated in the comprehensive opening contradiction and later lexical and conditional tests.

coverageAudit.majorLine: Institutional conduct and whether church wrongdoing bears on divine revelation
coverageAudit.omissionRationale: Cross-examination about Eucharist and individual sinners is omitted as a separate move because it develops the same institution-versus-members distinction covered by these three exchanges.

coverageAudit.omissionRationale: Locomotive-energy elaboration is omitted as a repetition of the power/external-source challenge; Horn's necessary-locomotive answer is represented through his combined clarification and original complete arguments.

coverageAudit.majorLine: Resurrection challenges from contradictions, natural alternatives, women witnesses, and visionary appearances
coverageAudit.omissionRationale: All four are retained because they attack distinct independently assessable warrants: source consistency, the attributed alternative, embarrassment, and bodily character.

coverageAudit.majorLine: Moral grounding through universal commands versus objective harm
coverageAudit.omissionRationale: The extended idolatry and utilitarian hypotheticals are omitted as cross-examination elaborations; the selected moves preserve each side's positive account and concrete application.

Both openings, both first rebuttals, both second rebuttals, both cross-examinations, and both closings have selected substantive moves. Moderator logistics, microphone trouble, timekeeping, applause, jokes, personal compliments, and audience-directed rhetoric are omitted.

coverageAudit.majorLine: Excluded audience Q&A and dependent answers
coverageAudit.omissionRationale: Events between 4,534,000 and 6,594,000 ms are entirely excluded by explicit editor approval. No claim, response, silence inference, or closing support is drawn from that interval.

speakerAttributionReview.correctedApologyReversal: Events 1030–1036 are read as Barker's immediately corrected slip: after first saying he would ask God for forgiveness, he corrects himself to say he would want God to apologize. No move treats the first wording as an uncorrected concession.
speakerAttributionReview.remainingUncertainty: No selected move has material unresolved speaker attribution. Whisper supplies no automatic names, but uninterrupted speeches and the complete question-answer sequences support high confidence. Recognition uncertainty in verse numbers, Greek/Hebrew forms, names, and the closing number is preserved and is not treated as participant error.
speakerAttributionReview.closingIndependence: Each selected closing move states its own retained premise: Horn restates the empty-tomb and appearance evidence; Barker restates the women-at-tomb, narrative-difference, and visionary-appearance arguments. None relies on an excluded audience question or answer.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: Counts were recomputed from the moves array. Small asymmetries follow the source: Horn presents three distinct metaphysical constructions plus a combined clarification, Barker develops four nonmergeable resurrection critiques, and the institutional/moral section contains Barker's separate institutional and secular-grounding lines. No numerical symmetry target controlled selection.

sections.rationale: Horn's first-cause, present-change, and contingency constructions have different starting facts and inferential routes; the fourth row is a later, independently assessable clarification answering quantum-vacuum and act-potency objections and cannot be merged into an opening without erasing responsiveness.

Barker's four rows address distinct warrants: narrative consistency and corroboration, misattributed group hallucination versus a grief alternative, the alleged embarrassment of women witnesses, and whether appearance reports are bodily or visionary. Merging them would hide separate targets and later replies.

Horn's four rows are independently assessable: opening accommodation/war hyperbole, later genre plus narrative survival, lexical disaster plus compensation, and cross-examination reliance on independent evidence plus authority over life. Each answers a different premise or stage of Barker's case.
